terminal.description: A shell in your workspace: node run.mjs <file> runs a query file against a fresh copy of the bakehouse database.

tasks.title: Spot the dear products in each category
tasks.description:
Tobias wants to know which products cost more than is usual for their own category. A loaf is not dear just because it costs more than a croissant.

In `queries/1-above-average.sql`, return `name`, `category` and `price` for every product whose price is **above the average price of products in the same category**. Sort by `category` from A to Z, then by `price` from highest to lowest.

Work the averages out inside the query. The hidden dataset has different prices, so typed-in numbers will fail.
nextSteps: Write a query that returns the average price of one category.
Use it as a subquery in WHERE for that one category.
Make the subquery follow the category of the outer row.
Add the sort and compare with the averages from the previous chapter.
hints: A subquery in parentheses that returns one value can stand anywhere a number can.
The subquery needs to know which category the outer row has. Give the outer table an alias so the inner query can refer to it.
Inside the subquery, filter with WHERE category = p.category, where p is the alias of the outer products table.

tasks.title: List the cafes that buy cake
tasks.description:
Tobias is launching a new cake and wants to tell the cafes that already buy cakes.

In `queries/2-cake-buyers.sql`, return `name` and `town` of every cafe that has **at least one delivered order containing a product in the `cake` category**. Each cafe appears **once**, however many cakes it bought. Row order does not matter.

Use `EXISTS` with a subquery. The check compares your rows with the expected rows on the shipped data and on a hidden dataset.
nextSteps: Write a query that lists the cake items in delivered orders for one cafe id.
Wrap it in EXISTS inside a query on cafes.
Connect the inner query to the outer cafe.
Check that no cafe appears twice.
hints: Joining cafes straight to orders and items gives one row per cake bought, so busy cafes repeat.
EXISTS (subquery) is true when the subquery returns at least one row. What it selects does not matter, so SELECT 1 is common.
Inside EXISTS, join orders, order_items and products, and add o.cafe_id = c.id to the conditions along with the status and category.

tasks.title: Find the cafes that spend above average
tasks.description:
Odile wants to offer a discount to the cafes that spend the most.

A cafe's spend is the sum of `quantity * price` over the items in its **delivered** orders, using the product's current price. Consider only cafes with at least one delivered order.

In `queries/3-big-spenders.sql`, return:

- `cafe`: the cafe's name
- `spend`: its spend, rounded to 2 decimals

for every cafe whose spend is **above the average spend of those cafes**. Sort by `spend` from highest to lowest. Compare unrounded values; round only in the final SELECT.

Use a common table expression (`WITH`) for the per-cafe spend. The check compares rows and their order on the shipped data and on a hidden dataset.
nextSteps: Write a query that returns cafe_id and spend for every cafe with delivered orders.
Put it in a WITH block and give it a name.
Select from that name, keeping cafes above the average of the same name.
Join to cafes for the name, then round and sort.
hints: Break it into two questions: what did each cafe spend, and what is the average of those numbers?
A WITH block works like a named table for the rest of the query, and you can read it more than once, including inside a subquery.
In the final query: FROM your named result, JOIN cafes, and WHERE total > (SELECT AVG(total) FROM your named result).
